title: Explain application of marketing principles within an alternative and dynamic agricultural marketing environment

lessons.title: Marketing principles for agricultural products
lessons.html:
What is marketing?

Marketing is everything a farm does to get its product to customers who want it, at a price that gives a profit. It is more than selling: it starts with understanding what the customer needs before you plant or breed.

The marketing mix (4 Ps)

  • Product: what you sell, including quality, grade, size, packaging and certification. Example: Class 1 tomatoes in 6 kg cartons.
  • Price: what the buyer pays. It must cover cost per unit plus a margin, and it is influenced by supply, demand and competitors.
  • Place: where and how the product reaches the buyer: farm gate, fresh produce market, supermarket, abattoir, co-operative, export.
  • Promotion: how buyers learn about the product: branding, signboards, social media, relationships with buyers, farmers' markets.

Supply and demand

Agricultural prices move with supply and demand. When many farmers harvest at the same time, supply rises and prices fall. In a drought, supply falls and prices may rise. Planning planting dates to harvest when supply is lower can earn better prices.

Understanding the customer

  • What quality and size do they want?
  • How much, how often and when?
  • Do they need certification, such as SA-GAP, GLOBALG.A.P. or organic?
  • How do they pay, and how quickly?

Quality is marketing

A buyer who receives consistent, well-graded, clean produce on time will come back and may pay more. Poor grading, bruising or late delivery damages the farm's reputation. Every worker who harvests, grades or packs is part of marketing.

lessons.title: Alternative markets in a changing environment
lessons.html:
A dynamic market environment

Agricultural markets keep changing. Prices, consumer tastes, input costs, exchange rates, weather and regulations all shift. Since deregulation of agricultural marketing in South Africa in the 1990s, farmers sell in open markets rather than through statutory control boards, so they must actively choose and manage their markets.

Alternative market channels

ChannelAdvantagesChallenges
National fresh produce markets (e.g. Johannesburg, Tshwane)Large volumes, open price discoveryPrices fluctuate daily; commission and transport costs
Supermarkets and retailersSteady volumes, contractsStrict standards, certification, programmed supply
Farm stalls and farmers' marketsHigher price per unit, direct customer contactSmall volumes, labour to staff
Informal traders and hawkersCash sales, flexible qualityVariable volumes, price pressure
Contract farming and processorsPrice agreed upfront, reduced riskMust meet contract specs and volumes
Co-operatives and group marketingBargaining power, shared transportNeeds trust and good management
Online and social media salesDirect reach, brandingDelivery logistics, payment security
ExportAccess to large markets, foreign currencyPhytosanitary rules, certification, exchange rate risk

Managing risk

  • Spread sales across more than one channel.
  • Use contracts or forward pricing where available.
  • Watch price information from markets and industry bodies.
  • Add value (packaging, processing) to reach new customers.

Applying the principles

For each channel, adjust the 4 Ps: a farm stall may sell mixed boxes at a premium with friendly service, while a supermarket wants uniform packs and reliable volumes.

Key points

  • Marketing starts with the customer's needs.
  • The 4 Ps are product, price, place and promotion.
  • Supply and demand drive farm prices.
  • Many alternative channels exist, each with pros and cons.
  • Spread risk and adapt the marketing mix to each channel.
